haze.note: bakery and bath-furnace smoke, stronger in the afternoon

spring.note: April: mild days, spring showers, the Favonius in the afternoons, mist on the Tiber at dawn

summer.note: hot and clear; thunderstorms over the hills inland

winter.note: rain and cold clear days; no snow in the city

look.light: honey-gold with a warm smoke haze; dusk is Rome's signature, gold not orange

capitolium.title: Capitolium
capitolium.text: Rome's greatest temple: three cellae for Jupiter, Juno and Minerva behind Corinthian columns of Pentelic marble, rebuilt by Domitian with gilded bronze roof tiles and a bronze chariot on the pediment. Generals ended their triumphs here, and the year's first vows are made here.
capitolium.epithet: Temple of Jupiter Best and Greatest

arx.title: Arx
arx.text: The Capitol's northern summit, where augurs watched the birds and Juno's geese once warned of the Gauls. The mint stood near the temple of Juno Moneta, and 'money' still carries her name.

tabularium.title: Tabularium
tabularium.text: A massive tufa base with an arcaded gallery of Doric half-columns, looking down the length of the Forum. The state's records and the bronze tablets of its laws were kept on the Capitol.

concord.title: Aedes Concordiae
concord.text: A temple whose cella runs across its width behind a six-column porch. Inside is a gallery of famous statues and paintings; the Senate sometimes met here.

vespasian.title: Templum Vespasiani
vespasian.text: A Corinthian temple on a high podium below the Tabularium, raised by Domitian to his deified father and brother.

saturn.title: Aedes Saturni
saturn.text: One of Rome's oldest temples, Ionic columns on a high podium. The state treasury, the aerarium, is kept in its podium. In December Saturn's feast turns masters into servants for a few days.

rostra.title: Rostra
rostra.text: A curved platform faced with the bronze rams of captured warships and crowded with honorary statues. Beside it stands the Golden Milestone, from which the roads of the empire were measured.

curia.title: Curia Iulia
curia.text: A tall brick hall with a plain gabled front and bronze doors. About six hundred senators meet here to pass decrees and judge their peers; their prestige is great, their power the emperor's to share.

lapis_niger.title: Lapis Niger
lapis_niger.text: A square of black paving behind a low fence marks an ancient, half-forgotten shrine. Some Romans said Romulus was buried here; others named a shepherd or a hero.

aemilia.title: Basilica Aemilia
aemilia.text: A two-storey arcade of white marble with shops along its front: a covered hall for business, money and law on the north side of the Forum.

forum_square.title: Forum Romanum
forum_square.text: Travertine paving set with honorary columns and statues, the well-head of the Lacus Curtius and, as Pliny says, a fig, an olive and a vine growing in the square. A schoolmaster teaches his pupils under an awning here in the mornings.

julia.title: Basilica Iulia
julia.text: A great two-storey arcaded hall where the centumviral court hears cases about inheritance. Idlers scratched gaming boards into its steps while they waited, and you can still find them.

castor.title: Aedes Castoris
castor.text: A temple of eight Corinthian columns on a very high podium, vowed after the battle of Lake Regillus. Its podium held offices and strongrooms; three of its columns still stand.

lacus_iuturnae.title: Lacus Iuturnae
lacus_iuturnae.text: A basin fed by the nymph's spring, with statues of the Dioscuri and their horses, where the twins were said to have watered their mounts. Its water was used in sacred rites.

divus_julius.title: Aedes Divi Iulii
divus_julius.text: Built where the people burned Caesar's body in 44 BC. Its speakers' platform carries the rams of ships from Actium; a round altar sits in a niche at its front.

regia.title: Regia
regia.text: A small, very old building, said to be King Numa's house and later the seat of the chief priest. The calendar's records and the sacred shields of Mars were kept here.

vesta.title: Aedes Vestae
vesta.text: A round temple of twenty Corinthian columns under a conical roof with an opening for the smoke. Inside burns the fire of Rome, tended day and night by the Vestal Virgins; men may not enter. On the Parilia people fetch the ashes for their fumigations here.

vestals.title: Atrium Vestae
vestals.text: A two-storey courtyard house with long pools, home of the six Vestal Virgins who serve for thirty years. Statues of the senior Vestals line the court.

piperataria.title: Horrea Piperataria
piperataria.text: Domitian's brick warehouses with small barred windows, for pepper and spices brought from India across the Red Sea and through Egypt.

arch_titus.title: Arcus Titi
arch_titus.text: A single marble arch on the Via Sacra. Inside, reliefs show Titus's triumph and the spoils of the Temple of Jerusalem, destroyed in AD 70, with the menorah carried shoulder high. For Rome's Jewish community it is a monument to loss, not glory.

venus_roma.title: Templum Veneris et Romae
venus_roma.text: Hadrian designed this vast double temple on the Velia himself, begun about 121 on the city's birthday: Venus faces east, Roma west, back to back. Treadwheel cranes lift column drums from rows on the ground; it will be dedicated in 135 and finished by 141.
venus_roma.epithet: Temple of Venus and Roma, a building site

colossus.title: Colossus
colossus.text: A colossal bronze statue made for Nero and turned into the Sun god with a radiate crown, perhaps 30 to 35 metres tall. To make room for the new temple, Hadrian had it moved upright with the help of elephants. The amphitheatre will one day take its name from it.

meta_sudans.title: Meta Sudans
meta_sudans.text: A tall conical fountain of brick faced with marble; water runs down its sides into a round basin where the processional routes meet.

colosseum.title: Amphitheatrum Flavium
colosseum.text: Three storeys of eighty arches and an attic, 48 metres high, with statues in the upper arches and masts for the great awning. Some fifty thousand people come here for gladiators and animal hunts. The name Colosseum is medieval, from the statue beside it.

trajan_forum.title: Forum Traiani
trajan_forum.text: The newest and grandest forum: a vast paved square with a gilded bronze Trajan on horseback, colonnades with statues of captive Dacians and hemicycles on both sides, paid for with Dacian gold.

basilica_ulpia.title: Basilica Ulpia
basilica_ulpia.text: A huge hall with columns of coloured marble and gilded bronze roof tiles, closing the north side of Trajan's Forum. Courts sit inside, and slaves were freed here before a magistrate.

trajan_column.title: Columna Traiani
trajan_column.text: A hundred Roman feet of Luna marble wound with a spiral relief of the Dacian wars, some 2,500 figures in 23 turns, and a bronze Trajan on top. His ashes rest in its base, between a Greek and a Latin library.

trajan_temple.title: Templum Divi Traiani
trajan_temple.text: Hadrian's temple to Trajan, shown north of the Column where the traditional reconstruction places it; recent excavations have questioned where it stood.

trajan_markets.title: Mercatus Traiani
trajan_markets.text: A semicircle of brick shops in tiers climbing the Quirinal, with a vaulted hall above and the street people now call the Via Biberatica running through it: oil, wine, spices, cloth and offices.

augustus_forum.title: Forum Augusti
augustus_forum.text: The temple of Mars the Avenger stands against a huge grey tufa firewall that keeps the Subura's fires away. In the porticoes stand Aeneas, Romulus and the great men of Rome, each with his deeds inscribed beneath.
augustus_forum.epithet: Forum of Augustus and Mars Ultor

caesar_forum.title: Forum Iulium
caesar_forum.text: Caesar's narrow colonnaded square with the temple of Venus Genetrix, mother of his family, restored by Trajan in 113, and the bankers' hall beside it.

nerva_forum.title: Forum Transitorium
nerva_forum.text: A narrow forum where the old street into the Subura ran; columns stand close to the wall under a frieze of women's crafts and the myth of Arachne. The temple is Minerva's.

pacis.title: Templum Pacis
pacis.text: Vespasian's garden square with long water channels and flower beds, porticoes full of famous art, a library, and the spoils of Jerusalem, among them the menorah.

palatine_tiberiana.title: Domus Tiberiana
palatine_tiberiana.text: The older palace on the Palatine's north edge, begun under Tiberius, its brick substructures rising high over the Forum.

domus_flavia.title: Domus Flavia
domus_flavia.text: Domitian's palace of state: a vast throne hall, a basilica, a dining hall between fountains and a peristyle round an octagonal fountain maze. The emperor receives the Senate here.

domus_augustana.title: Domus Augustana
domus_augustana.text: The private palace, whose curved façade and high brick substructures look down over the Circus Maximus. Our word 'palace' comes from this hill, the Palatium.

palatine_stadium.title: Hippodromus Palatii
palatine_stadium.text: A sunken garden shaped like a stadium, with porticoes, plane trees and fountains, for walks in the shade.

apollo_palatinus.title: Aedes Apollinis Palatini
apollo_palatinus.text: Augustus's temple of Luna marble beside his house, sacred to his patron god, with a famous Greek and Latin library.

house_augustus.title: Domus Augusti
house_augustus.text: A modest house with painted rooms where the first emperor lived for forty years, preferring simplicity to palaces.

casa_romuli.title: Casa Romuli
casa_romuli.text: A small thatched hut of wattle and daub, piously rebuilt whenever it is damaged, where Romulus was said to have lived. Today is the city's birthday, and people bring garlands.

lupercal.title: Lupercal
lupercal.text: A cave shrine at the foot of the Palatine where the she-wolf nursed Romulus and Remus. In February the Luperci run round the hill from here at the Lupercalia.

circus_maximus.title: Circus Maximus
circus_maximus.text: A long arena with tiered seats for some 150,000, shops in its outer arcades, twelve starting gates and a central barrier with Augustus's obelisk, seven bronze dolphins and seven eggs to count the laps. Four factions race: Red, White, Green and Blue.

porta_capena.title: Porta Capena
porta_capena.text: An old tufa gate of the Servian wall under an aqueduct branch, always dripping. The Via Appia begins here. Rome itself has no circuit wall in 126; carts wait here for dusk.

portunus.title: Aedes Portuni
portunus.text: A small Ionic temple on a podium by the old river port, sacred to the god of harbours. It still stands.

hercules_victor.title: Aedes Herculis Victoris
hercules_victor.text: A round temple of twenty white marble columns in the cattle market by the river, the oldest marble building in Rome to survive.

ara_maxima.title: Ara Maxima
ara_maxima.text: Where Hercules, the story goes, rested his cattle by the Tiber. Merchants vowed a tenth of their profits here.

tiber_island.title: Insula Tiberina
tiber_island.text: The island is faced with travertine like a ship's prow and stern, with an obelisk for a mast. The healing god Aesculapius has his temple here; the sick sleep in its porticoes, hoping for a cure in a dream.

pons_fabricius.title: Pons Fabricius
pons_fabricius.text: A stone bridge of 62 BC joining the island to the left bank. It is still in use.

pons_cestius.title: Pons Cestius
pons_cestius.text: The stone bridge of the first century BC from the island to Transtiberim, the quarter across the Tiber, rebuilt many times since.

pons_aemilius.title: Pons Aemilius
pons_aemilius.text: Rome's first stone bridge, carrying the road from the cattle market across to Transtiberim and the Via Aurelia.

pons_sublicius.title: Pons Sublicius
pons_sublicius.text: The oldest bridge, always rebuilt in wood: no iron may be used in it. Here, the story goes, Horatius held off the Etruscan army.

horrea_galbana.title: Horrea Galbana
horrea_galbana.text: Long warehouses round courtyards where grain brought up the Tiber from Portus is measured, recorded and stored for the monthly distribution and the bakers.

testaccio.title: Mons Testaceus
testaccio.text: A hill made of broken oil amphorae from southern Spain, emptied at the wharf, smashed and laid in lime. It is about half its later height and will keep growing until the third century.

emporium.title: Emporium
emporium.text: A travertine wharf with mooring posts, treadwheel cranes and stacked amphorae, the warehouse rows of the Porticus Aemilia behind it. Barges towed up from Portus unload grain, oil, wine and marble here. The great vaulted Porticus is shown as rows of warehouses.

marcellus.title: Theatrum Marcelli
marcellus.text: Augustus's theatre for his nephew, its curved travertine façade of arcades in Doric and Ionic storeys. Some 15,000 people watch comedies and mimes here.

octavia.title: Porticus Octaviae
octavia.text: A colonnaded precinct round temples of Jupiter and Juno, full of Greek art. Pliny saw a seated statue of Cornelia, mother of the Gracchi, in a portico of this area.

pantheon.title: Pantheum
pantheon.text: Hadrian has just rebuilt it: sixteen granite columns, Agrippa's name kept in the inscription, and a brick rotunda under a dome 43 metres across, covered in bronze tiles and open to the sky through its oculus. It is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome.

pantheon_court.title: Area Panthei
pantheon_court.text: A colonnaded court before the portico, where the Pantheon is entered. Seen from here the rotunda hides behind the tall temple front.

matidia.title: Templum Matidiae
matidia.text: Hadrian's temple to his deified mother-in-law, Matidia, built after 119 beside the Pantheon: the first temple in Rome to a deified woman of the imperial family, some think.

agrippa_baths.title: Thermae Agrippae
agrippa_baths.text: Rome's first great public baths, with a domed hall, vaulted rooms and an exercise yard, beside the Stagnum, an artificial lake fed by the Aqua Virgo.

saepta.title: Saepta Iulia
saepta.text: Built for the people's voting assemblies, the long colonnaded hall now holds luxury shops. Its building is not drawn yet: you see its paved court lined with stalls and columns.

iseum.title: Iseum Campense
iseum.text: An Egyptian-style sanctuary with obelisks and sphinxes, where shaven priests in linen shake the sistrum. Its buildings are not drawn yet: a paved court with columns and an altar stands in for it.

stadium_domitian.title: Stadium Domitiani
stadium_domitian.text: A stadium for Greek-style athletic contests; its shape survives as the Piazza Navona. Here you see its long arena of trampled earth with statues along the middle.

pompey_theatre.title: Theatrum Pompei
pompey_theatre.text: Rome's first stone theatre, with a temple of Venus Victrix on top of the seating and a great portico garden behind its stage, where Caesar was killed. Shown as its paved half-round and the garden's plane trees.

trajan_baths.title: Thermae Traiani
trajan_baths.text: Apollodorus built these vast baths on the Oppian in 109: great halls round a central block, exedrae, exercise yards and gardens in a walled precinct. Its hall is not drawn yet: you see a paved block of vaulted bath halls with yards and gardens.

tarpeian.title: Saxum Tarpeium
tarpeian.text: The sheer tufa cliff of the Capitol over the Velabrum, from which traitors were thrown in the old Republic.

aqua_claudia.title: Aqua Claudia
aqua_claudia.text: Tall arches of rusticated tufa and brick carry Nero's branch of the Claudia across the Caelian to the Palatine. Rome has ten aqueducts in 126; the curator of the waters and his public slaves keep them running.

castra_praetoria.title: Castra Praetoria
castra_praetoria.text: The walled brick camp of the emperor's guard, some ten thousand men, on the edge of the city. Guards drill outside its gates.

suburban_villa.title: Villa suburbana
suburban_villa.text: A rich family's country house with its vineyard and kitchen gardens just outside the city, run by a steward.
suburban_villa.epithet: A villa on the Via Appia

synagogue.title: Synagoga
synagogue.text: Rome's Jews had their own synagogues and burial places, and one community lived across the Tiber. Its form is not known from excavation, so it is shown as a modest house.

hadrian.title: Hadrianus
hadrian.text: He has walked the empire from Britain, where his wall is being built, to Syria. Back in Rome he is rebuilding the Pantheon and designing a temple to Venus and Roma himself; his portraits always show a full beard. Where he spent 21 April 126 is not recorded: the game imagines him here for the festival.

sabina.title: Vibia Sabina
sabina.text: Trajan's grand-niece and Hadrian's wife, she travelled with him across the provinces and received the title Augusta. Coins carry her portrait and her high coiled hairstyle, copied by fashionable women. Whether she was in Rome today is not recorded; the game imagines her here.

antinous.title: Antinous
antinous.text: A youth from Bithynia, beloved of Hadrian and with him from about 124. After his death in the Nile in 130, Hadrian made him a god and founded a city in his name. His presence in Rome in 126 is likely but not recorded: today the game has him riding out.

marcus.title: Marcus Annius Verus
marcus.text: Born on the Caelian, this serious little boy turns five on 26 April. Hadrian will call him 'Verissimus', most truthful. In 161 he becomes emperor as Marcus Aurelius and writes, in Greek, a private book of reflections that people still read. Today he watches the procession.

apollodorus.title: Apollodorus of Damascus
apollodorus.text: He built Trajan's Forum, Column and Baths and a bridge over the Danube. Cassius Dio, writing a century later, says he mocked Hadrian's design for Venus and Roma and paid with exile and death; many historians think the story gossip. Whether he was in Rome in 126 is unknown.

juvenal.title: Iuvenalis
juvenal.text: He hates the noise: carts at night, crowds by day, tiles falling from tall blocks, rich patrons who keep clients waiting at dawn. He said the people want only two things, bread and circuses. You will find him grumbling in the Subura or in a morning queue.

suetonius.title: Suetonius Tranquillus
suetonius.text: Once Hadrian's secretary for letters, now writing lives of the Caesars full of habits, sayings and scandal. He was dismissed about 122, the story goes, for a lapse of manners toward the empress. He works among the books of Trajan's libraries.

mesomedes.title: Mesomedes
mesomedes.text: A freed lyre-singer from Crete who composes hymns for Hadrian. Some of his songs survive with their melodies written above the words, among the very few ancient tunes we can still read and sing. In the evenings he plays in the palace gardens.

soranus.title: Soranus of Ephesus
soranus.text: Trained in Alexandria, he practises in Rome and writes about childbirth, the care of mothers and newborns, and what makes a good midwife. His book was copied and used for more than a thousand years. You may find him among the sick on the island.

diocles.title: Gaius Appuleius Diocles
diocles.text: A driver of twenty-two from Lusitania who began racing in 122. By the end of his career his monument will list 1,462 victories and a fortune greater than many senators'. This year he drives four horses for the Whites.

vestalis_maxima.title: Virgo Vestalis Maxima
vestalis_maxima.text: The senior of the six women who guard Vesta's fire and Rome's sacred objects for thirty years each. They have seats of honour at the games, may free a condemned man they meet by chance, and keep the wills of emperors. Her name in 126 is not known.

plotina.title: Pompeia Plotina
plotina.text: Praised for her modesty and her learning, she backed Hadrian's succession when Trajan died and supported the Epicurean school in Athens. She died about 122, and Hadrian honoured her with a temple. At dusk she seems to walk again in her husband's forum.

trajan.title: Traianus
trajan.text: The Senate called him optimus princeps, the best of rulers. Conqueror of Dacia, builder of this forum, its markets and the harbour at Portus, he died in 117. His Column tells his wars in 2,500 figures and his ashes rest in its base; at dusk his memory stands beside it.

numa.title: Numa Pompilius
numa.text: Rome's second king, by legend, gave the city its priests, its calendar and the cult of Vesta, advised, they said, by the nymph Egeria in a sacred grove. The Regia was called his house. At dusk a bearded king seems to pass between the Regia and the fire.

scipio.title: Scipio Africanus
scipio.text: Before any public business, Livy says, he climbed to Jupiter's temple and sat there alone with the god, and some Romans whispered he was Jupiter's son. He defeated Hannibal at Zama in 202 BC. Before dawn his memory still sits at the Capitolium.

caesar.title: Divus Iulius
caesar.text: Gaius Julius Caesar, conqueror of Gaul and dictator, was killed by senators in 44 BC. The people burned his body here in the Forum, and on that spot rose his temple, the first to a Roman made a god. At dusk his memory stands by it, wreathed in laurel.

cicero.title: Marcus Tullius Cicero
cicero.text: The greatest speaker of the Republic spoke from these Rostra against Catiline and Mark Antony. After his murder in 43 BC, Antony had his head and hands fixed here. At dusk he still seems to speak, silently, to the emptying Forum.

dioscuri.title: Castor et Pollux
dioscuri.text: After the battle of Lake Regillus, the story goes, two young riders were seen watering their horses at Juturna's spring, announcing the victory, then vanishing. Rome built them a temple beside the spring. Very rarely, at dawn, two riders seem to stand there.

aeneas.title: Aeneas
aeneas.text: Son of Venus, he carried his father Anchises out of burning Troy and led his son Ascanius to Italy, the poet Virgil tells. Augustus placed this statue group in his forum, facing Romulus, at the beginning of Rome's story and his own family's.

romulus.title: Romulus et Remus
romulus.text: Set adrift on the flooded Tiber, the twins were nursed by a she-wolf in the Lupercal cave below the Palatine. Romulus founded the city on 21 April, traditionally in 753 BC: today is its birthday. His statue stands in the Forum of Augustus, carrying a defeated king's armour.
romulus.epithet: Sons of Mars (a statue and a shrine)

cloelia.title: Cloelia
cloelia.text: A hostage of the Etruscan king, she escaped across the river with other girls, and Rome honoured her with a statue on horseback on the Via Sacra. Whether one stood here in 126 is uncertain: Dionysius found the old one gone, and some said it showed Valeria.
cloelia.epithet: The girl who swam the Tiber (a statue)

cornelia.title: Cornelia
cornelia.text: Daughter of Scipio Africanus, she refused a king, educated her children herself and called her sons, the reformers Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus, her jewels. Pliny saw her seated statue in a portico here; an inscribed base survives, though where it stood is debated.

claudia_helpis.title: Claudia Helpis
claudia_helpis.text: Born a slave, freed by her mistress, Claudia Helpis now runs her own counter of hot chickpeas, lentils, wine and bread in the Subura. Freed men and women ran a large share of Rome's shops, and many proudly carved their trade on their tombs.

vibius_primus.title: Lucius Vibius Primus
vibius_primus.text: Primus's donkeys turn the lava mills before dawn; by sunrise the loaves are stamped with his mark. Each month the state hands out free grain to some two hundred thousand citizens, and many of them bring it to bakers like him.

aelius_eutyches.title: Publius Aelius Eutyches
aelius_eutyches.text: An imperial freedman, he counts the grain ships' cargoes for the prefect of the grain supply and checks the warehouses' tallies at the Horrea Galbana. Under Hadrian more senior posts went to equestrians, but freedmen still ran the daily paperwork of the empire.

apion.title: Apion
apion.text: Apion came from a village in Egypt and joined the fleet. In a real letter, a recruit of that name told his father he had arrived safely at Misenum and been given a Roman name. Today he has come up the river on a grain barge.

mulvius.title: Quintus Mulvius
mulvius.text: Mulvius steers a barge up the Tiber from Portus, towed by men and oxen on the bank path: a few days against the current for some thirty-five kilometres, much quicker back down with the stream. He knows every sandbank between Portus and the Emporium.

flavius_valens.title: Titus Flavius Valens
flavius_valens.text: Valens walks the streets at night with buckets, axes and blankets. Fire is the great terror of a city of wooden floors and oil lamps. A law let informally freed slaves who served six years in the watch, later three, earn full citizenship.

felicula.title: Felicula
felicula.text: Felicula fetches water from the fountain twice a day and plays with walnuts on the pavement with her brother. Her mother dyes cloth; her father treads it clean in the vats. More than anything she wants to see the races.

rufina.title: Rufina
rufina.text: Rufina's family has lived across the Tiber for generations among dockers, potters and traders from the East. Rome's Jews had their own synagogues and burial places; the Arch of Titus, with its spoils of Jerusalem, is not a monument they love.

sextus.title: Sextus
sextus.text: Sextus, from Thrace, carries his master's litter across the city every morning with seven others. Rome had no uniform for slaves: the Senate once rejected one, Seneca says, in case the slaves saw how many they were. In the afternoons he runs errands for the household.

iulia_ianuaria.title: Iulia Ianuaria
iulia_ianuaria.text: Ianuaria has delivered half the children of her street. Soranus wrote that a good midwife must be literate, calm, and have soft hands and short nails. Inscriptions remember several Roman midwives by name. She walks her rounds on the Aventine.

law.title: Ius
law.text: In the Basilica Iulia advocates plead before the centumviral court, and jurists give written opinions on hard cases. Roman law grew from statutes, the praetors' yearly edicts and those opinions into a body of rules and reasoning that later Europe studied again. Hadrian will soon have the jurist Salvius Iulianus fix the praetor's edict in a permanent form, about 130.

concrete.title: Opus caementicium
concrete.text: Lime mortar mixed with volcanic ash, dug round Rome and named for Puteoli near Naples, sets hard, even under water. Poured with rubble behind neat brick faces, it let Romans vault halls and baths of a size no one had built before. The Pantheon's dome uses lighter stone toward the top; it is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.

aqueducts.title: Aquae
aqueducts.text: Ten aqueducts bring water to Rome in 126, the newest Trajan's of 109, some in channels more than eighty kilometres long. The water runs down gentle slopes in covered channels, crosses valleys on arcades, and ends in settling tanks and distribution towers that feed fountains, baths and the few houses granted a private pipe. Most Romans carry theirs from a street fountain.

cursus_publicus.title: Cursus publicus
cursus_publicus.text: Paved roads run from Rome to every province, measured by milestones from the Golden Milestone in the Forum. Along them the state post keeps relay stations where official couriers change mules and horses, with inns nearby. The Via Appia, begun in 312 BC, runs from the Porta Capena all the way to Brundisium.

calendar.title: Fasti
calendar.text: Caesar reformed Rome's muddled calendar in 46 BC with the help of Greek astronomers: 365 days and a leap day every fourth year. Days are counted back from the Kalends, Nones and Ides, and each is marked for business or for the gods. Today, the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, is the Parilia.

maps.title: Orbis pictus
maps.text: Augustus's friend Agrippa had the known world drawn and set up in a portico on the Campus Martius, so that Romans could see their empire from Britain to the Euphrates. It has not survived; ancient writers who used it describe its distances and provinces.

greek_learning.title: Paideia
greek_learning.text: Educated Romans speak Greek as well as Latin. Greek teachers, doctors, architects and musicians fill the city, and Hadrian himself loves Greek culture and wears a Greek-style beard. Children of good families learn Homer with a Greek tutor and rhetoric from a master.

literature.title: Litterae
literature.text: Books are papyrus rolls copied by hand, sold in shops near the Forum and read aloud. Trajan's Forum has a Greek and a Latin library facing the Column. Juvenal writes his satires and Suetonius his lives of the Caesars in these years.

annona.title: Annona
annona.text: Rome eats far more grain than Italy grows. The prefect of the grain supply brings it by sea from Egypt, Africa and Sicily to Portus, then by barge up the Tiber to the warehouses. Each month some two hundred thousand citizens holding a token collect five measures of free grain.

night_carts.title: Plaustra nocturna
night_carts.text: A law of Caesar's time banned heavy carts from the city's streets for most of the day, probably until the tenth hour, except for public building work and a few sacred processions. So the carts wait at the gates and come rumbling in at dusk, and Juvenal complains that no one can sleep.

baths.title: Thermae
baths.text: For a small coin anyone may bathe: undress, exercise in the yard, sweat in the hot rooms, soak in the warm, plunge in the cold, and be oiled and scraped with a strigil. The baths fill after the eighth hour. Hadrian, says the Historia Augusta, separated men's and women's bathing.

factions.title: Factiones
factions.text: Chariot teams race for four companies known by their colours, and all Rome takes sides. Four horses run seven laps round the barrier; a dolphin tips at each lap. Star drivers, most of them slaves or freedmen, grow rich and famous.

amphitheatre_games.title: Munera
amphitheatre_games.text: On game days crowds file in through numbered arches, the awning is drawn, and the water organ and horns play. Gladiators fight in pairs of different arms, and wild animals from Africa are hunted. The game shows only the outside and the sounds.

religion.title: Religio
religion.text: Romans keep peace with the gods by doing things right: a prayer said exactly, an animal offered with music, the entrails read. Every house has its Lares, every crossroads a shrine, and the city honours its own gods beside Isis, Cybele, Mithras and the emperors made divine.

sacrifice.title: Sacrificium
sacrifice.text: The priest covers his head, a piper plays the tibia so no ill-omened sound is heard, wine and incense go on the fire, and the victim is struck. Its entrails are inspected for signs; the meat is cooked and shared. Sacrifice is how Rome talks to its gods.

parilia.title: Parilia
parilia.text: The Parilia was the shepherds' feast of Pales, kept on 21 April, the day Romulus founded the city. The flocks are smoked clean at twilight and young people leap the burning straw. Hadrian's coins of 121 celebrate the city's 874th birthday with games, and by about AD 200, Athenaeus says, the day was 'now called' the Romaia.

freedmen.title: Liberti
freedmen.text: Slaves in Rome were often freed, by will or by purchase. Freed men and women took their former owner's family name, became citizens, ran shops and workshops, and some grew rich; their children were born free. Many proudly recorded their trades on their tombs.

housing.title: Insulae
housing.text: Most Romans rent rooms in brick apartment blocks of four or five storeys, shops on the ground floor and the cheapest rooms at the top, without water or kitchens. Trajan limited their height to sixty feet; fires and collapses were feared, as Juvenal complains.

plebs.title: Plebs
plebs.text: Ordinary citizens in coloured or undyed tunics: shopkeepers, craftsmen, labourers and clients. The toga is for formal business and the games.

client.title: Cliens
client.text: A citizen who owes his patron loyalty and his vote, and gets help, food or a little money in return. He calls at dawn in his toga and follows the patron to the Forum.

senator.title: Senator
senator.text: Broad purple stripes on his tunic, a white toga, black senatorial shoes and often a short beard in Hadrian's fashion. Clients and slaves follow him.

lictor.title: Lictor
lictor.text: An attendant carrying the fasces, a bundle of rods, ahead of a magistrate. Inside the city the axe is taken out of the bundle.

advocate.title: Advocatus
advocate.text: A speaker in a toga pleading a case about an inheritance before the centumviral court in the Basilica Iulia.

gaming_board.title: Tabula lusoria
gaming_board.text: Idlers scratched gaming boards into the basilica's steps and played with counters while the courts sat inside.

rostra_speaker.title: From the Rostra
rostra_speaker.text: Magistrates and orators address the crowd from the speakers' platform, as the great men of the Republic did.

school.title: Ludus
school.text: A schoolmaster teaches reading, writing and sums to a few pupils with wax tablets under an awning in the Forum, from dawn until midday.

seller.title: Venditrix
seller.text: A woman selling from a shop or stall, one of the many women who kept Rome's small trade going.

porter.title: Baiulus
porter.text: A porter carrying loads through streets where carts may not go by day.

enslaved.title: Servus
enslaved.text: Perhaps a fifth to a third of Rome's people are enslaved. They wear no special dress; you know them only by the work they are made to do.

matron.title: Matrona
matron.text: A married woman in a long stola with her mantle drawn over her head outside, her hair dressed high in the empress's fashion.

vestals_order.title: Virgines Vestales
vestals_order.text: Six priestesses in white with woollen bands who tend Vesta's fire, fetch water from a spring and prepare the sacred salt meal.

flamen.title: Flamen
flamen.text: A priest of one god, in a heavy cloak and the apex, a cap topped with a spike of olive wood.

ara_maxima_rite.title: At the Great Altar
ara_maxima_rite.text: Rites for Hercules at his altar by the cattle market; merchants vow him a tenth of their profits.

urban_cohort.title: Cohortes urbanae
urban_cohort.text: Soldiers of the urban cohorts keep order in the streets under the Prefect of the City. In the city they usually go without armour.

syrian.title: Syrus
syrian.text: A merchant from Syria in a long tunic and mantle, trading in glass, purple cloth, dates and balsam.

freedman.title: Libertus
freedman.text: A freed man or woman running a shop: Rome's small trade was largely in their hands.

tabularium_clerk.title: Scriba
tabularium_clerk.text: Clerks of the record office climb to the Capitol to copy and file the state's documents.

geese.title: Anseres Iunonis
geese.text: Juno's sacred geese, kept on the Capitol since they cackled a warning when the Gauls climbed the hill by night.

mason.title: Faber
mason.text: Masons set marble drums and capitals in the peristyle of the new temple.

treadwheel.title: Magna rota
treadwheel.text: Men walk inside a great wooden wheel to wind the rope of a crane and lift blocks that weigh several tonnes.

bricklayer.title: Structor
bricklayer.text: Gangs lay the brick facing and pour mortar and rubble behind it: Roman concrete walls rising course by course.

labourer.title: Operarius
labourer.text: Free and enslaved labourers fetch bricks, mortar and rubble for the building site.

site_cart.title: Plaustrum
site_cart.text: Ox carts for public building may run by day; most other heavy carts must wait for dusk.

fountain.title: Lacus
fountain.text: Street fountains stand every few blocks, running day and night; women and children fetch water and news there.

praetorian.title: Praetoriani
praetorian.text: The emperor's guard, some ten thousand men camped at the Castra Praetoria, posted at the palace in shifts.

german_guard.title: Equites singulares
german_guard.text: Horsemen of the emperor's own mounted guard, many recruited from Germanic peoples of the Rhine frontier.

courtier.title: Amicus principis
courtier.text: Friends and officials of the emperor waiting on business at the palace.

gardener.title: Topiarius
gardener.text: A gardener clipping box and bay into shapes and keeping the roses of a great house.

stables.title: Stabula
stables.text: Stable hands groom, feed and harness the racehorses of the four factions near the starting gates.

docker.title: Saccarius
docker.text: Dockers carry sacks and amphorae from the barges to the warehouses; they had their own guilds.

horrea_clerk.title: Horrearius
horrea_clerk.text: A clerk who measures, records and seals each load of grain that enters the warehouse.

testaccio_work.title: On the mound
testaccio_work.text: Workers break emptied oil amphorae and lay the sherds in neat terraces, sprinkled with lime against the smell.

warehouse.title: Horrea
warehouse.text: Warehouse porters move amphorae of oil and wine between the wharf, the stores and the decanting floor.

hauler.title: Helciarius
hauler.text: Men and oxen on the bank path haul barges upstream from Portus on long tow ropes.

egypt.title: Aegyptius
egypt.text: Egyptian sailors crew the grain ships that bring perhaps a third of Rome's bread across the sea.

swallows.title: Hirundines
swallows.text: The swallows are back with the spring, swooping over the river and the rooftops.

cattle_market.title: Forum Boarium
cattle_market.text: Cattle are driven in to the market by the river, as they have been since the city was young.

aesculapius.title: Incubatio
aesculapius.text: The sick sleep in the porticoes of Aesculapius on the island, hoping the god will send a cure in a dream.

baker.title: Pistor
baker.text: The baker kneads, shapes, stamps and bakes before dawn; donkeys turn his lava mills.

mill_donkey.title: Asinus
mill_donkey.text: Blindfolded donkeys walk round and round, turning the hourglass-shaped lava mills that grind the grain.

fuller.title: Fullo
fuller.text: Fullers tread cloth in vats of water, fuller's earth and stale urine, then rinse, brush and dry it.

dyer.title: Infector
dyer.text: Dyers soak cloth in vats of madder red, woad blue or saffron yellow; true purple comes only from Tyre.

glass.title: Vitrearius
glass.text: A glassblower gathers molten glass on a pipe and blows cups and flasks, a craft come from Syria.

smith.title: Faber ferrarius
smith.text: A smith at his forge making nails, tools, hinges and fittings for the quarter.

taberna.title: Taberna
taberna.text: A shop open to the street with a masonry counter, closed at night with wooden shutters, selling bread, oil, cloth or lamps.

thermopolium.title: Thermopolium
thermopolium.text: A street counter with sunk jars of hot food and wine; most flats have no kitchen, so people eat here.

weaver.title: Textrix
weaver.text: A woman weaving wool at home, one of the many who made Rome's cloth.

stoker.title: Fornacator
stoker.text: Slaves feed the bath furnaces with wood from before dawn to keep the hot rooms hot.

vigiles.title: Vigiles
vigiles.text: Seven cohorts of firemen and night watchmen, with buckets, axes, hooks and blankets soaked in vinegar.

women.title: Mulieres
women.text: Women fetch water, shop, work at looms and counters, visit neighbours and keep the household going.

children.title: Pueri et puellae
children.text: Children play with walnuts, knucklebones and hoops in the street; boys wear a bulla, girls a lunula.

salutatio.title: Salutatio
salutatio.text: At dawn clients in togas queue at their patrons' doors for the morning greeting, a little gift and the day's business.

litter.title: Lectica
litter.text: A curtained litter carried by eight slaves, the way the rich cross the crowded city by day.

popina.title: Popina
popina.text: Late diners and drinkers leave the street counters with lamps; the night watch keeps an eye on them.

dogs.title: Canes
dogs.text: Dogs guard doors (cave canem, says the mosaic) and roam the streets for scraps.

cats.title: Feles
cats.text: Cats have become common in Roman houses and shops, good at keeping mice from the grain.

aquarius.title: Aquarius
aquarius.text: Public slaves of the water office clear channels, patch pipes and open the valves.

synagogue_community.title: Iudaei
synagogue_community.text: Jews of the Transtiberim community trade, weave and worship in their own synagogues across the river.

gaul.title: Gallus
gaul.text: A trader from Gaul in trousers and a hooded cloak, selling wine and woollen cloaks.

moor.title: Maurus
moor.text: A Moorish horseman from Africa; Moorish cavalry under Lusius Quietus served in Trajan's wars.

theatre.title: Theatrum
theatre.text: Comedies, mimes and pantomime dancers draw crowds to the theatres of the Campus Martius.

farmer.title: Agricola
farmer.text: Farmers and tenants work the market gardens, fields and olive yards round the city.

vinedresser.title: Vinitor
vinedresser.text: Vine-dressers prune, tie and hoe the vines on the hills outside the city.

villa.title: Vilicus
villa.text: The steward of a villa, often himself a slave, runs the estate for its owner.

shepherd.title: Pastor
shepherd.text: Shepherds bring their flocks to graze on the hills and the Campagna; the Parilia is their festival.

tombs.title: Sepulcra
tombs.text: Burial is forbidden inside the city, so tombs line the roads leading out of it; families visit with offerings.

mules.title: Muli
mules.text: Pack mules carry loads by day, when carts are banned from the streets.

fish_market.title: Piscator
fish_market.text: River fishermen land their catch for the stalls of the cattle market.

legions.title: Milites
legions.text: The legions are on the frontiers; in Rome you see veterans, recruits and soldiers on errands.

compitum.title: Compitum
compitum.text: A shrine of the Lares at a crossroads, tended by the neighbourhood's magistrates; its lamp is lit at dusk.

graffiti.title: Inscriptiones
graffiti.text: Walls carry painted notices and scratched graffiti: election appeals, jokes, love notes and insults.

performer.title: Circulator
performer.text: A juggler or piper draws a small ring of watchers in a portico.

starlings.title: Sturni
starlings.text: At dusk flocks of birds wheel over the Tiber before settling for the night.

weather_april.title: April showers
weather_april.text: A spring shower: gutters spout, warm paving steams, and sometimes a rainbow stands over the Palatine.

nundinae.title: Nundinae
nundinae.text: Market day, every eighth day in Rome: farmers come in, stalls fill the squares, and in the game the races follow in the afternoon.

senate.title: Senatus
senate.text: Senators with lictors and clients arrive at the Curia for a session.

wedding.title: Nuptiae
wedding.text: At dusk the bride is led to her new home by torchlight, pipers playing, nuts thrown to the children.

night_cart_role.title: Plaustrarius
night_cart_role.text: A carter bringing building stone and goods into the city by night.

cursus_role.title: Viator
cursus_role.text: A traveller on the Via Appia, resting at the relay stations between Rome and the south.

parilia_rite.title: The shepherds' rite
parilia_rite.text: Ovid tells it: at twilight the fold is swept and the ground sprinkled with water, green boughs hung up, and the sheep purified with smoke of sulphur, olive wood, pine and juniper. The shepherd prays to Pales four times, facing the east, and washes his hands in dew.

romaia.title: The birthday procession
romaia.text: In the morning the priests, the Vestals and the Senate walk from the Forum to the new temple of Venus and Roma, begun on this day in 121, for a sacrifice. Hadrian and Sabina lead it, as the game imagines them here.

vinalia.title: Vinalia Rustica
vinalia.text: On 19 August Jupiter is asked to protect the vintage to come; Varro says the flamen of Jupiter cut the first grapes.

vestalia.title: Vestalia
vestalia.text: In June Vesta's temple is opened to women, who walk barefoot to it; bakers rest and their donkeys wear garlands.

saturnalia.title: Saturnalia
saturnalia.text: In December masters serve their slaves at table, everyone wears the freedman's felt cap, and friends give candles and clay figurines.

reaper.title: Messor
reaper.text: Gangs of reapers cut the wheat of the Campagna with sickles in early summer; the straw is left long and the ears go to the threshing floor.

ploughman.title: Arator
ploughman.text: After the first autumn rains the ox plough turns the fields and the wheat is sown for next summer.

grape_picker.title: Vindemiator
grape_picker.text: In September and October the grapes of the Janiculum and the Campagna are cut, trodden and pressed, and the must poured into jars.

olive_picker.title: Oleae lector
olive_picker.text: Olives are gathered from November into December, beaten or picked, and pressed for the year's oil.

haymaker.title: Faenisex
haymaker.text: The country calendars put the hay harvest in June: meadows mown and the hay dried for the winter's animals.

shearer.title: Tonsor ovium
shearer.text: Sheep are washed and shorn in May, before the heat, as the farm calendars carved in stone advise.

floralia.title: Floralia
floralia.text: From late April into May the games of Flora are held: plays, races and flowers, with goats and hares let loose in the Circus.

october_horse.title: Equus October
october_horse.text: A two-horse chariot race on the Campus Martius; the right-hand horse of the winning pair is sacrificed to Mars.

kalends.title: Kalends of January
kalends.text: The new consuls take office, vows are made for the emperor on the Capitol, and people give small gifts of sweets and lamps for luck.

strings.pompa: The procession of the games leaves the Capitol for the Circus.
strings.races: The races begin: four teams, seven laps.
strings.parilia_purification: Twilight: the folds are swept and the flocks purified with smoke.
strings.bonfires: The young leap three times over the burning straw.
strings.salutatio: Dawn: clients queue at their patrons' doors for the morning greeting.
strings.trial: A case is being heard in the Basilica Iulia.
strings.senate: Senators are arriving at the Curia.
strings.market_day: Market day: farmers have come in and the stalls are full.
strings.arena: Horns and the water organ: a game day at the amphitheatre.
strings.dole: Citizens with tokens queue for their monthly grain.
strings.grain_fleet: A grain barge has come up the Tiber from Portus.
strings.vestals: The senior Vestal walks to the Circus with her lictor.
strings.guard: The guard is changed at the palace.
strings.night_carts: Dusk: the carts kept out by day rumble in through the gate.
strings.fire: Fire in an apartment block: the watch runs with buckets.
strings.funeral: A funeral leaves the gate for the tombs of the Via Appia.
strings.wedding: Torches and pipes: a bride is led to her new home.
strings.decorate_zone: A peristyle garden of a house on the Caelian, waiting for box hedges, roses and a fountain.
strings.floralia: The Floralia: flowers, plays and games in the Circus.
strings.october_horse: The October Horse: a chariot race on the Campus Martius.
strings.ludi_plebeii: The Plebeian Games: the Circus fills again.
strings.kalends: The Kalends of January: the new consuls go up to the Capitol.
strings.braziers: Braziers glow in the shops and at the crossroads shrines.
strings.dusting: A dusting of snow on the roofs this morning. It will be gone by noon.
strings.vintage: The grapes are trodden on the Janiculum.
strings.season_turn.spring: The swallows are back under the eaves.
strings.season_turn.autumn: The grapes are in: the vintage begins.
strings.season_turn.winter: Braziers glow in the doorways against the cold.
